A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToolACE and retain identifiable matching methods and experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToolACE results on BFCL-v1/v2, verification and data-composition ablations, model-scaling experiments, and general-capability evaluations.

after.justification: v2 reports original BFCL-v3 and API-Bank results, retained experimental analyses, and additional training-data comparisons, component ablations and in-context-learning experiments in Appendices E and G.

M1.justification: v1 uses query/API embedding similarity to assess complexity and select generated data. v2 Section 2.2 introduces a target-model loss evaluator, a suitable complexity range estimated from prior data, and feedback that dynamically simplifies or complicates generated queries. This substantially changes complexity control within the retained multi-agent generator.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates function calling on BFCL-v1/v2. v2 introduces BFCL-v3 evaluation with explicit multi-turn testing and adds API-Bank Call and Retrieval+Call results, extending coverage to retrieving unknown APIs. The general-capability benchmarks and reported 26,507-API pool remain.

E2.justification: The BFCL comparator set changes substantially: v2 includes xLAM-8x22b-r, xLAM-8x7b-r and FireFunction-v2, while v1's Functionary entries disappear. v2 also adds GPT-4 to the general-capability comparison, controlled ToolLLM/xLAM training-data baselines in Appendix E.1, and a retrieved three-shot LLaMA baseline in Appendix G.

E3.justification: BFCL evaluation moves to v3, with subsequent main studies described as using non-live categories. Complexity sampling changes to loss-ranked 60,000-example subsets, and diversity grouping changes from K-means to the API context tree. New studies introduce fixed 25,000-example budgets, evaluator controls and BGE-retrieved three-shot prompts. These are reported protocol changes; unchanged plots do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds loss-versus-complexity analyses in Figure 2, data-type and evaluator ablations in Appendix E, and in-context-learning failure analysis in Appendix G. v1's formalized-thinking ablation, verification pass-rate plot, and dataset/complexity distribution analyses are removed. The main verification, complexity, diversity and backbone studies remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's loss-distribution plots characterize differences among samples rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: v1's BFCL-v1/v2 leaderboard results of 91.41% and 85.77% are replaced by BFCL-v3 results of 59.22%, ranked third, plus API-Bank scores of 75.94% Call and 47.41% Retrieval+Call. Different benchmarks prevent interpreting these as performance gains or losses. Tables 6–9 add substantial comparison and ablation results; earlier formalized-thinking results disappear. The main verification, complexity and diversity ablation values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of complexity changes from negative cosine similarity between BGE embeddings in v1 Equation 1 to model-dependent mean token negative log-likelihood in v2 Equation 1. This is a substantive but localized definition change; neither version develops formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 makes capability-adapted generation using the learner as evaluator a central contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. It newly claims priority for highlighting API synthesis as a route to function-calling generalization and extends its empirical contribution to API-Bank. The broad claim that an 8B model can compete with GPT-4 in function calling remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit limitations concerning evaluator cost, scalability, sampling bias and difficulty learning harder examples, plus acknowledged general-reasoning gaps to GPT-4. Appendices E and G add explanations of evaluator–learner mismatch, effects of removing data types, and hallucinations induced by tools appearing in few-shot demonstrations.

D1.justification: v2 adds benchmark composition and scoring descriptions, concrete BFCL/API-Bank prompts, and BGE retrieval instructions. It removes v1's generation pseudocode, JSON/format-conversion examples, and explicit majority-vote, loss-mask and thinking-exclusion details. This substantially changes reproducibility documentation. The LoRA hyperparameter table is retained in Appendix C, and model/data access information remains equivalent.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated related-work section distinguishing tuning-free tool use, tool-augmented tuning and data synthesis. New comparisons include ReAct, Toolformer, API-BLEND, Self-Instruct and WizardLM, while model-oriented data selection supports the revised complexity approach. Research positioning expands substantially beyond v1's introduction and comparison table.

P1.justification: The introduction and dialog-generation narrative are extensively rewritten, with explicit contribution bullets added. Verification becomes part of Section 2, the standalone data-analysis section disappears, experimental details move to Appendix C, and related-work, additional-experiment and limitations sections are introduced. This is substantial reorganization beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline and retained experimental charts, restructures the BFCL table, and adds loss-distribution plots, API-Bank and appendix result tables, and prompt examples. Numerous dataset/format illustrations disappear. The API context subtree is retained in Appendix A, while the scaling figure loses its relevance panel and gains numerical annotations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's BFCL leaderboards: API-Bank broadens testing, while fixed-backbone, fixed-budget dataset comparisons and data-type/evaluator ablations directly examine the value of the training data and design choices. Explicit limitations better establish applicability boundaries. Some dataset statistics, formalized-thinking evidence and generation details are lost, but the controlled evidence and clearer qualifications provide a substantial net improvement.
